GeneretiCoreBrowserUpscale:
# ꘅ ONNX upscale

Experimental browser-only Real-ESRGAN worker: local image cleanup/upscaling on the viewing device. GeneretiCore owns optional downloads and execution; Genereti supplies streams and preview/output views.

## Start here

Open **15 - Browser ONNX upscaling**. Load a local image/video/GIF in the 2D stream and press its Play control. The sample explicitly resizes to 256×256. ↓ downloads about 34.7 MB of verified public ONNX models and runtime files; ↑ loads and warms the selected model/backend; ▶ starts inference; Ⅱ pauses; × unloads the worker and its GPU resources. Nothing downloads or runs on workflow load. No HF account or student conversion is needed.

Choose AnimeVideo for illustrated content or General for ordinary images. WebGPU and WASM CPU are separate explicit choices; unavailable/failed GPU execution reports an error, with no silent backend or cloud fallback. Browser/device support and speed vary. An active browser is required; this is not headless Python inference or an assistant provider.

## Input and output

Connect any shared live IMAGE source, directly or through Image Preview. Borrowed source frames are copied immediately. Keep delivery Live. Inputs must be 2–256px per side; larger sources need an explicit upstream resize. The worker predicts 4x, then high-quality canvas resizing gives source/2x/4x output. Alpha composites on white. Output retains the last completed image during loading, inference, pause and unload. A single pending frame replaces older waiting frames; pause/source changes discard stale results and release subscriptions. There is no previous-frame smoothing or recursive refinement yet.

Comfy Queue deliberately reports that an active browser is required. Use the separate native **Real-ESRGAN upscale** node for queued image processing. Browser output is a live IMAGE frame; it is not automatically an input to an arbitrary queued Python node.

The dot toggles timing text. Total measures worker round-trip including preparation and output; Model measures the ONNX session call, including runtime-managed transfers. The FPS estimate is 1000/mean Total, rather than measured display/source FPS. Cold load includes warmup. WebGPU work can compete with creative rendering even in a worker.

## Credits and provenance

[Model sources, checksums, tool versions and PyTorch parity](https://huggingface.co/languel/genereticore-upscalers-coreml/tree/300be594b8faf75dc297799c57950f763422bc89/onnx). Real-ESRGAN by Xintao Wang and contributors, [BSD-3-Clause full license](https://huggingface.co/languel/genereticore-upscalers-coreml/blob/300be594b8faf75dc297799c57950f763422bc89/onnx/LICENSE). Independently exported from official AnimeVideo-v3 and General-x4v3 weights; no upstream endorsement. ONNX Runtime Web 1.24.3 by Microsoft and contributors, MIT; full notice bundled in licensing/ONNX-Runtime-LICENSE.txt. Models and runtime binaries stay outside Git, with pinned hashes in the download catalog.

Cross-browser, classroom hardware, long-running motion quality and device-loss behavior need wider testing. SDXS/Turbo, detection, segmentation and assistant providers are separate future browser integrations.

# ꘅ Choice to Value

Maps a selected label to an authored finite number for a creative control.

## Inputs, outputs and controls

Inputs: choice (STRING socket) and values_json. Output: value (FLOAT). Every selected label needs an entry; booleans and nonfinite numbers are rejected.

## Small example

Use `{"blue":210,"orange":30}`. Connect value to a livecode paletteHue socket using HSB degrees (0–360).

## Requirements and limits

No model runs here. Units come from the destination control. A model decision updates this mapping only after connected workflow Run.
GeneretiCoreDecision:
# ꘅ Local Decision

Ranks your fixed set of allowed labels for a situation and question. It returns controls, not executable code.

## Inputs, outputs and controls

Inputs: model, prompt (state), choices_json (allowed labels), max_tokens and optional question. Outputs: choice, decision_json (scores/probabilities) and metrics. ↓ downloads; ▷ runs the graph; ϟ previews locally; □ cancels a local preview request.

## Small example

State: “A quiet moonlit lake with soft ripples.” Question: “Which palette fits?” Choices: `["blue", "orange"]`. Wire choice to ꘅ Choice to Value.

## Requirements and limits

d1 is text-only, requires macOS 15+ and the d1 helper, accepts 2–8 labels and at most 256 combined input tokens, and ignores max_tokens. Qwen requires macOS 27+ and uses answer-slot scores. Scores are uncalibrated; artistic judgment is not guaranteed.

GeneretiCoreTutorial0:
# GeneretiCore Tutorial 0

# Tutorial 0 · From a situation to a creative decision

You do not need to know machine learning or JSON to start. This tutorial introduces the idea behind our workflows, explains the nodes you will meet, and gives each experiment a purpose. Read it before opening the practical examples. The first exercise does not run a model.

## What are we making?

We are making a small artwork whose color can respond to a description of a scene. Imagine two descriptions: “a quiet moonlit lake” and “a lively sunrise festival.” Our artwork has two authored palettes: blue and orange. We ask a local model which palette fits the description, then turn that answer into the hue of a moving circle.

The model does not draw the circle, write the sketch, or invent new controls. You authored the artwork and the possible palettes. The model makes one bounded choice inside that design. This is a useful pattern for interactive art: a changing situation becomes a small, inspectable control.

## What is a decision model?

A decision model reads a **state** (a description of the current situation), a **question**, and a set of **allowed options**. It returns a distribution over those options and a selected answer.

For our palette demo:

- State: “A quiet moonlit lake with soft ripples.”
- Question: “Which palette best fits this scene?”
- Allowed options: `blue`, `orange`.
- Possible result: blue has a larger score than orange, so blue is selected.

The words blue and orange are labels you define. They are not automatically colors in Comfy. A later mapping node assigns each label a number that the artwork understands.

A chat model generates a sequence of words. A specialist decision model such as d1 instead evaluates the allowed answers in a single forward pass, without generating a written reply. Our Qwen example uses a different method: it scores answer slots with a small language model. Both can feed the same creative graph, but their scores have different meanings and their quality must be evaluated separately.

## Why choose the options ourselves?

Allowed options define the boundaries of your artwork. If you offer only blue and orange, the decision cannot introduce a third palette or execute a command. You might instead offer `slow` and `fast`, `sparse` and `dense`, or three named scenes. Choose options that correspond to controls you actually designed.

Changing an option changes the question the model is answering. It is not a way to train the model. For your first experiment, keep the two palette labels unchanged and edit only the scene description. This lets you compare answers while the artwork's meaning stays stable.

Later, adding a label such as violet also requires adding a numeric mapping. A label alone does not tell p5 what to render. The label, the mapping, and the creative control form a contract between your graph's parts.

## Scores, probabilities, and uncertainty

A score indicates how much the model favors an option for this particular input. A distribution assigns a value to each allowed option. In a normalized distribution, the values add up to one. For example, blue 0.8 and orange 0.2 selects blue.

This does **not** mean that 80 percent of people would prefer blue, or that blue is objectively correct. Creative choices are contextual and subjective. A model can be confidently unhelpful. Two almost equal scores tell you the decision is close; you may decide to keep the previous palette instead of switching on every small change.

Our d1 adapter applies the upstream model's published calibration temperatures before converting logits to probabilities. The result labels its method `d1_temperature_scaled`. Calibration from the model's training/evaluation setting does not certify reliability for your creative task. Qwen's result is labeled `answer_slot_softmax_uncalibrated`; the supplied-score exercise is `normalized_uncalibrated_scores`. Read the method alongside the numbers rather than treating all distributions as equally reliable.

## What is JSON?

JSON is a plain-text format for named data. Curly braces group an object, a name followed by a colon introduces a field, and square brackets hold a list. Quotation marks identify text. You will see a result shaped like this:

```json
{"choice":"blue","scores":{"blue":0.8,"orange":0.2}}
```

`choice` is the selected label. `scores` contains a value for every allowed label. Our validator adds a normalized `probabilities` object and a `probability_kind` field explaining the method.

The Text / JSON Viewer offers **Tree**, **Pretty**, and **Minified**. Tree lets you expand or collapse an object such as scores. Pretty shows indented text. Minified shows compact JSON for copying. These are three views of the same data; switching views never changes the decision. Plain text is displayed as plain text. The viewer does not run AI.

## Exercise 1 · Read a decision, without AI

Open **01 - Read a decision - no model**. This is a demonstration of the result contract, not a decision-model inference demo. The **ꘅ Decision Scores Validator** receives a small, already-written result and checks it. The connected **Text / JSON Viewers** display the selected label and distribution.

Press top Run, then expand scores in the tree. The numbers are supplied by us; nothing was inferred. We use this exercise so you can learn what an answer looks like before waiting for downloads or interpreting a model.

An optional second experiment changes the supplied scores. Change blue from `0.8` to `0.1`, leave orange at `0.2`, and also change `choice` from `blue` to `orange`:

```json
{"choice":"orange","scores":{"blue":0.1,"orange":0.2}}
```

Press Run. Orange now has the larger score, so the selected label is orange. The normalized probabilities are about `0.333` for blue and `0.667` for orange. The supplied scores do not need to sum to one.

If you change only blue's score, the JSON still says `"choice":"blue"`. Editing a number does not update another JSON field automatically. With blue at `0.1` and orange at `0.2`, that answer contradicts itself. The validator shows “Needs correction” inside the node when the selected choice contradicts the scores. Connected outputs are skipped and our JSON viewers are marked “Not updated”; no Comfy execution error dialog is needed. Correct the JSON and press Run again. This shows the safety contract: downstream controls should receive a complete, consistent answer. Editing these example scores does not teach or fine-tune a model. In the real demos, the model supplies the scores for you.

## Meet the nodes

`ꘅ` substitutes for GeneretiCore in visible node labels; `ꘇ` substitutes for Genereti. Class names, workflow node types and model catalog identifiers retain their Latinized names.

The node title contains its actual display type followed by its job in this graph. Hover the main node dot to see its saved Comfy class and description. Select a node and open Node Info for its description. Custom titles are descriptions; they do not change the underlying class.

- **ꘅ Tutorial** (`GeneretiCoreTutorial`): opens this lesson. No inference.
- **ꘅ Decision Scores Validator** (`GeneretiCoreValidateDecision`): validates supplied decisions. No inference.
- **ꘅ Local Decision** (`GeneretiCoreDecision`): sends a state, question and allowed options to the selected local model.
- **ꘅ Choice to Value** (`GeneretiCoreChoiceValue`): looks up a selected label in an authored dictionary and outputs a number. No inference.
- **ꘅ Text / JSON Viewer** (`GeneretiCoreResult`): displays connected results. No inference.
- **ꘅ Local Text** (`GeneretiCoreText`): generates words with Qwen; it is not the same task as selecting a fixed option.
- **ꘅ Local Vision** (`GeneretiCoreVision`): describes one connected image with Qwen3-VL. The current d1 Core ML conversion does not accept images or audio.
- **ꘇ livecode**: runs your p5 artwork in the browser. It renders independently of model inference.

## Exercise 2 · A real local d1 decision

Open **07 - d1 - scene to artwork palette**. This demo connects a real decision model to a moving artwork. It requires Genereti public as well as GeneretiCore.

Read the state, question and allowed labels on Local Decision. If d1 is missing, use its download arrow. Downloads are explicit and cached locally. The contributor build requires the d1 helper; model assets and compiled caches are kept outside the source repository.

Press the top Comfy Run. Follow the graph: Local Decision selects a label; Choice to Value maps blue to 210 or orange to 30; the numeric wire sets p5's `paletteHue` control. The viewer displays the distribution, and the timing viewer reports loading and prediction time. No model-written code is evaluated.

Try the quiet moonlit lake, then change only the state to “The scene is entirely orange: orange lights, orange walls and an orange sunset.” Run again and compare the selected palette and distribution. These clear fixtures exercise the complete wiring. Then try an energetic sunrise festival: in one local test the model still chose blue for that warm scene. This is a useful disagreement to inspect, not something the demo should hide. Ask whether each choice serves your artwork. Record disagreements rather than assuming the model must be right. You may change the mapping values to explore different colors while keeping the same decision labels.

## Which Run does what?

Top Run, or the inference node's triangle, queues the connected graph and updates downstream results. The lightning glyph submits a local preview inside the inference node only. Use top Run for these exercises.

The p5 editor's Run applies your creative code. Its saved artwork starts rendering when you open the workflow. The walkthrough node's Run opens narrated steps and node highlights. Neither of these buttons queues model inference.

The download arrow prepares the selected model; it does not run inference. Opening a workflow never starts inference, camera, microphone, or audio. Our models run locally, with no automatic hosted fallback.

## Timing and two clocks

The artwork keeps animating while a model works. Browser rendering and native model inference have separate clocks. Inference runs in an isolated native helper through a bounded queue, away from rendering and audio threads.

The first run can compile and load the model and is much slower than a warm prediction. `prediction_ms` measures the model call; `end_to_end_ms` also includes the surrounding request work. `generated_tokens: 0` is expected for d1. It is choosing an answer, not writing a sentence. Compare cold and warm results instead of promising live responsiveness from a single model-card number.

The image walkthrough takes one queued frame from the moving sketch. It does not analyze every animation frame. For future continuously changing inputs, stale results must be handled explicitly: the latest-state policy suppresses obsolete answers, and a previous visual result can remain displayed while the next request works.

## A useful next experiment

Design one control with a small set of meaningful states. Write the state and question plainly. Define the options, map each option to a control, and inspect both the answer and its distribution. Change one part at a time. Keep a manual override and a visible result so that the artist can understand what the system did.

These examples demonstrate wiring, local inference and creative control—not a benchmark or a guarantee of good judgment. Your evaluation is part of the artwork's design.
GeneretiCoreTutorial8:
# Tutorial 8 · ꘅ Blocks & Beats

This demo is a simplified self-playing Tetris simulation whose board state also conducts music. Open **08 - Blocks and Beats - decision arcade** in Comfy. The **ꘅ Decision Arcade · open Blocks & Beats** node opens the local demo with its ▦ button. **ꘇ lesson · walkthrough · press its Run** narrates the exercise. In the demo page, **ꘅ Local Decision · choose a legal placement** and **ꘅ Local Decision · choose the next music pattern** expose the two decision loops. These panel labels describe tasks; they are not additional registered Comfy classes.

Nothing starts merely by opening the workflow or page. Click **Start game** to start simulation/inference. **Start audio** is separate. Comfy's top Run does not start the game or sound.

## What does a decision model do here?

The authored game rules enumerate legal hard drops for the current piece. They measure the board after each drop: rows cleared, holes under occupied cells, total column height and unevenness. A fixed heuristic shortlists four good placements. d1 receives that compact situation, a question about the best drop, and labels A–D. It selects a label; the game looks up the already-validated placement. It never executes model-written game code.

This is already a helpful limitation: d1 cannot choose an illegal move. It can still choose a strategically poor move. The shortlist itself contains human assumptions. Ask whether minimizing holes and height is enough to play well, and whether the numeric summary loses useful spatial information. The demo does not use vision; only text features reach the current Core ML model.

Follow **ꘅ Local Decision · choose a legal placement**. The highlighted candidate is the selected answer. The JSON viewer contains scores and timings; Tree, Pretty and Minified change presentation, not data. Scores describe model preferences, not the objective value of a move.

## Three clocks

Rendering runs on the browser animation clock. One asynchronous move decision finishes before the next piece is committed; only one request is outstanding. A legal ghost drop animates while the native helper remains separate from the renderer.

Audio uses its own Web Audio scheduling clock. Every four pieces, and after a cleared row, the music decision reads stack height, holes and recently cleared rows. It chooses one of four authored patterns: calm, drive, tense or celebrate. The first piece also requests a music decision.

Follow **ꘅ Local Decision · choose the next music pattern**. While audio plays, a completed choice is staged as next. It becomes current at the next bar boundary. The previous pattern continues during inference. The ResultPair helper also rejects older revisions. With audio off there is no sounding bar, so the visual pattern preview can update immediately. These patterns are local synthesized notes and percussion; no Strudel source, samples or hosted music model are required.

Pause stops the game and invalidates pending inference, but audio continues until **Stop audio**. Reset cancels outstanding decisions and restores the same seed; it does not secretly switch the player. Errors pause with an inline status and no automatic cloud or heuristic fallback.

## Compare an authored player with d1

Choose **Authored heuristic · no AI**, then Start game. This chooses the highest heuristic utility directly, without model download or inference. Reset to seed 7, choose d1 and repeat. Use the same pace and number of committed pieces. Compare rows cleared, stack height and holes rather than just asking which animation looks smarter. Pausing retains the uncommitted piece.

The game uses all seven tetrominoes in a seeded seven-bag sequence. This teaching simulation omits manual controls, hold, wall kicks and competitive scoring. It is a demonstration of decision-to-control architecture, not a competitive Tetris agent.

## Model setup and boundaries

The d1 mode uses the existing locally tested Core ML backend on Apple silicon. Download the pinned model explicitly if missing; first compilation/loading can take much longer than a warm decision. The no-model player runs without a native helper. The browser calls the same loopback-only, same-origin API as other ꘅ nodes. Stop/Reset rejects late results, including those already submitted when the board changes. No camera, microphone or screen capture is involved.

The current catalog does not load ONNX models. The ONNX community d1 export is a promising separate backend, with custom token/marker handling and text, image and audio graphs. Supporting it requires pinned assets/runtime, license provenance, cancellation and parity checks against the existing decision contract. Published ONNX timings are not local measurements. See the [ONNX model card](https://huggingface.co/onnx-community/d1-omni-600M-ONNX).

## Experiments

- Watch the candidate features before revealing the model's answer. Which drop would you choose, and why?
- Compare a calm low stack with a high stack: does the music choice reflect the stated mapping?
- Start audio, then watch next wait until a bar. Pause the game and notice that music has a separate clock.
- Reset and compare d1 against the authored heuristic. A fast local model is not automatically a strong game player.
GeneretiCoreUpscale:
# ꘅ Real-ESRGAN upscale

Clean and enlarge low-resolution images locally with compact AnimeVideo or General Real-ESRGAN models. Try AnimeVideo for smooth graphic edges, and General for textured images; compare both on your source.

## Inputs, outputs and controls

IMAGE input; IMAGE output and JSON metrics. **model** chooses AnimeVideo or General. **scale** selects source-size cleanup, 2x or 4x output. Both models predict 4x internally; smaller output sizes use Lanczos downsampling. **passes** selects one prediction or two-pass same-image refinement. **feedback** blends the downsampled first result with the original before the second prediction (0 keeps the original; 1 uses the first result). It has no effect with one pass and stores no previous-frame history.

## Small example

Open **14 - Real-ESRGAN cleanup comparison**. Use each node's ↓ to download SDXS and the upscalers, then explicitly start SDXS and upscale with ▶. Compare the original 256px frame with the cleaned 512px frame. The dot toggles timings and shows state in its hover tip. Ⅱ pauses new processing and holds the last completed output. Models never start or download on workflow load.

For one queued frame, pause both inference nodes, choose Comfy Queue delivery on the source, generator and upscaler, then use Comfy Run. Queued metrics include load/wait, inference and total time. Live Total includes the local request, model, PNG encoding and browser decoding; FPS estimates 1000 / average Total and is not measured screen FPS.

## Requirements and limits

macOS 14+ Apple silicon, optional image dependencies and the Genereti companion for live delivery. ↓ installs both 256px and 512px model packages from the pinned public bundle. No student HF login or conversion is needed. Inputs must be 2–512px per side, including non-square images; larger input needs an explicit resize upstream. The appropriate package is selected automatically. Alpha composites on white. Queued batches are limited to four images. Live inputs use Genereti’s shared IMAGE subscription, including texture operators, streams and preview routing. GPU texture readback adds overhead; frames are copied before the callback returns.

Only one live native request runs at a time across generators and upscalers. Waiting frames are replaced by the newest input. Pause lets an active native call finish and discards its stale output. First use can compile/load the model and take noticeably longer. Two passes cost another prediction. No cloud inference fallback.

## Credits and licenses

[Public bundle, conversion provenance and complete notices](https://huggingface.co/languel/genereticore-upscalers-coreml). Real-ESRGAN by Xintao Wang and contributors, [official source](https://github.com/xinntao/Real-ESRGAN) and [official weights](https://github.com/xinntao/Real-ESRGAN/releases/tag/v0.2.5.0). BSD 3-Clause notices are retained. These are independently converted compact SRVGG models, not the much larger RRDB RealESRGAN_x4plus. General uses its ordinary weights; the optional upstream WDN interpolation is not included.
GeneretiCoreValidateDecision:
# ꘅ Decision Scores Validator

Checks supplied scores and selected choice. This node does not run AI.

## Inputs, outputs and controls

Inputs: choices_json and decision_json strings. Outputs: choice and normalized decision_json. Labels must match, scores must be finite and nonnegative, and choice must have a highest score. Invalid input explains the issue and blocks downstream outputs.

## Small example

Allowed labels `["blue","orange"]`; decision `{"choice":"blue","scores":{"blue":0.8,"orange":0.2}}`. Run, then change both scores and choice to compare outcomes.

## Requirements and limits

No model or Apple runtime needed. Scores need not sum to one; all-zero distributions are rejected. A previous downstream result is marked not updated when validation fails.
GeneretiCoreVision:
# ꘅ Local Vision

Describes one supplied image using local Qwen3-VL 2B.

## Inputs, outputs and controls

Inputs: model, image (IMAGE), prompt, max_tokens. Outputs: text and metrics. ↓ downloads the pinned model; ▷ runs the connected graph. This node has no separate image preview inference button.

## Small example

Connect ꘇ livecode image to image, ask “Describe the image briefly”, connect text to the viewer and press Run. Rendering continues independently of analysis.

## Requirements and limits

macOS 27+ Core AI helper required. One image per observation; batches are rejected. The image is resized to at most 1024 pixels per side. This is queued analysis, not continuous per-frame inference.
GeneretiCoreWelcome:
# Welcome to ꘅ GeneretiCore

GeneretiCore adds local inference to Genereti’s creative surfaces. Rendering, editing, preview display and inference are separate activities. Opening Help or a workflow does not download models or start inference.

## Inputs, outputs and controls

Use the header ? for this shared Reference, Contents and Assistant panel when Genereti is installed. Ask about this node prepares context and a draft; you choose when to send. Without Genereti, ? opens the local reference.

## Small example

Start with **01 - Read a decision - no model**. Run the supplied validator fixture and inspect its JSON. Then read Tutorial 0 and choose a model-backed example.

## Requirements and limits

Core AI text/vision/Qwen decisions require macOS 27+ Apple silicon and the contributor Swift helper. Text-only d1 requires macOS 15+ Apple silicon and its separate helper. SDXS and SD Turbo require macOS 14+ Apple silicon, optional image-runtime dependencies and existing converted packages. Linux can inspect docs and validate example graphs; it cannot run these Apple backends. No automatic cloud fallback. These are experimental contributor paths, not a verified student distribution.
GeneretiSDTurboGenerate:
# ꘅ SD Turbo generator

Remixes an image or follows Canny, depth or pose guidance using the migrated one-step Core ML engine. Stable ID: GeneretiSDTurboGenerate.

## Inputs, outputs and controls

Inputs: model_path, prompt, mode, seed, preprocess, strength, influence (control_scale), invert, movement and optional image. Outputs: image and metrics. Preprocess extracts Canny/depth; disable it for a prepared guide. Strength is image-remix noise (0.05–1), not guidance. Movement rotates seeded noise in Live; zero holds it.

## Small example

Open **11 - Livecode to SD Turbo** or **12 - Drawing to SD Turbo**. Use ↓ to download the public 256px + 512px bundle, choose image mode and strength 0.95, then press ▶. Optional Canny needs separately sourced control weights. Use Queue plus Comfy Run for a single frame.

## Requirements and limits

macOS 14+ Apple silicon and optional image dependencies required. ↓ explicitly downloads the verified public bundle; no HF login or conversion is needed. Guide modes need control_<mode> and turbo_residual_unet beside encoder/decoder/base UNet. Depth preprocessing requires its separately cached pinned model. Pose accepts a prepared guide and starts no device. Preview freeze/minimize does not stop inference. Pause prevents new requests and drops stale completion; it cannot interrupt an already running Core ML call. 512px image and Canny were tested locally on one Mac; broader parity and older OS validation remain pending. Powered by Stability AI; upstream use terms apply.

## Blank input during performance

Enable **Blank input** to use a second prompt when the connected image is a uniform background. The chevron shows or hides its field; collapsing does not disable the option. It starts disabled and is saved with the workflow. This works in Live and Comfy Queue. Detection happens before guide preprocessing or inversion and requires every pixel to be nearly the same color; even a small contrasting mark keeps the normal prompt. Text mode has no image to check.

Choose **Alternate prompt** to generate an empty scene (the default is “closeup flat white blank paper space pristine smooth emptiness”). Models may still invent shadows or texture. Choose **Solid white** for an exact white frame without inference while the input is blank. Drawing again automatically resumes the main prompt. The main prompt and held draft remain unchanged.

The bottom color dot shows the current state in its hover tip. Clicking it hides or shows the timings beside it. Timings are rounded averages updated once a second; errors remain visible.

## Credits and licenses

[Published bundle, upstream credits and complete license notices](https://huggingface.co/languel/genereticore-sd-turbo-coreml/blob/fd78b21b29cec891fb09d87c76233ddb44c6edb3/Notice.txt). SD Turbo by Stability AI; TAESD by madebyollin; CLIP and OpenCLIP contributors. Powered by Stability AI. The bundle preserves upstream license notices and source backlinks.

## Native sizes

Choose `256/unet.mlpackage` (SDXS) or `256/turbo_unet.mlpackage` (Turbo) for the faster 256px version. The corresponding `512/` path keeps 512px. Both use the same node; the explicit bundle download installs both size folders and shared text assets. 256px reuses the original 512-trained weights with smaller fixed shapes, so appearance can differ. Both resolutions were exercised on this Mac.

Live timings: Total includes input capture, the local request, inference, image decoding and publication. The FPS estimate is 1000 divided by average Total milliseconds; the delay between requests and screen refresh are excluded. Model measures the native pipeline, including prompt encoding and image decoding. Values are averaged and refreshed once per second.

## Connected live image sources

Live image input uses Genereti’s shared frame subscription. It accepts a started 2D stream or webcam, drawing, texture and Livecode sources, directly or through an Image Preview. Keep each node on Live delivery. The generator copies borrowed frames immediately and processes the latest available frame with one inference request at a time. Pausing or removing it releases its subscription; it does not start a camera automatically. Update Genereti and GeneretiCore together, then reload Comfy to obtain the shared bridge export. Comfy Queue still accepts ordinary IMAGE connections.
GeneretiSDXSGenerate:
# ꘅ SDXS generator

Generates images locally from text or a sketch with the migrated one-step Core ML engine. The node ID stays GeneretiSDXSGenerate for saved graphs.

## Inputs, outputs and controls

Inputs: model_path, prompt, mode (text/sketch), seed, influence (control_scale), invert, movement and optional image. Outputs: image and metrics. Model path sets native size and base/anime variant. Live/Comfy Queue chooses delivery; ▶ starts inference, Ⅱ pauses it. Prompt ϟ applies while typing; ↑ or Cmd/Ctrl+Enter commits a held draft.

## Small example

Open **09 - Livecode to SDXS** or **10 - Drawing to SDXS**. Use ↓ to download the public 256px + 512px bundle, leave sketch selected, then press ▶. A connected ꘇ image preview holds the latest completed frame while the next computes.

## Requirements and limits

macOS 14+ Apple silicon and optional image dependencies are required. ↓ explicitly downloads the verified public bundle; no HF login or conversion is needed. Sketch needs controlled_unet; anime needs its own controlled package. Only the first queued IMAGE is used; alpha composites on white. In-flight native work completes after pause; stale results are discarded. Live inference is loopback-only, bounded to one request at a time. No cloud fallback or model downloads on workflow load. 512px text/sketch and the live bridge were tested locally on one Mac; broader parity and older OS validation remain pending.

## Blank input during performance

Enable **Blank input** to use a second prompt when the connected image is a uniform background. The chevron shows or hides its field; collapsing does not disable the option. It starts disabled and is saved with the workflow. This works in Live and Comfy Queue. Detection happens before guide preprocessing or inversion and requires every pixel to be nearly the same color; even a small contrasting mark keeps the normal prompt. Text mode has no image to check.

Choose **Alternate prompt** to generate an empty scene (the default is “closeup flat white blank paper space pristine smooth emptiness”). Models may still invent shadows or texture. Choose **Solid white** for an exact white frame without inference while the input is blank. Drawing again automatically resumes the main prompt. The main prompt and held draft remain unchanged.

The bottom color dot shows the current state in its hover tip. Clicking it hides or shows the timings beside it. Timings are rounded averages updated once a second; errors remain visible.

## Native sizes

Choose `256/unet.mlpackage` (SDXS) or `256/turbo_unet.mlpackage` (Turbo) for the faster 256px version. The corresponding `512/` path keeps 512px. Both use the same node; the explicit bundle download installs both size folders and shared text assets. 256px reuses the original 512-trained weights with smaller fixed shapes, so appearance can differ. Both resolutions were exercised on this Mac.

Live timings: Total includes input capture, the local request, inference, image decoding and publication. The FPS estimate is 1000 divided by average Total milliseconds; the delay between requests and screen refresh are excluded. Model measures the native pipeline, including prompt encoding and image decoding. Values are averaged and refreshed once per second.
